idiom_name: strategy interface plus a context holding one concrete strategy (object or function value)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: declare one operation (or a small set of related operations) as the strategy interface, give every algorithm its own implementation of it, and let the context hold whichever implementation is current - injected at construction, replaced through a setter, or looked up in a registry by key. In languages with first-class functions the interface collapses into a function type and a strategy becomes a value; keep the explicit object whenever the strategy carries configuration, exposes more than one operation, or needs a name for logging, testing and configuration. The selection itself belongs to the client, a factory or the application wiring - never to the context - and strategies should be stateless per call or clearly documented about sharing and thread-safety. When the language supports Protocols or structural typing, prefer them over explicit inheritance to reduce coupling.
pitfalls: Letting the context construct its own concrete strategy hard-wires the algorithm again; inject it or take it from the wiring.
A stateful strategy shared between contexts (or threads) couples them through hidden mutable state.
Widening the strategy interface so every variant fits one shape - or letting the context test the concrete strategy type - destroys the substitutability that justified the pattern.
Using null to denote 'no strategy' scatters null checks through the code; provide a Null Object strategy instead.
Strategies that hold open connections, thread pools or other native resources must implement clean disposal; otherwise context refactoring or strategy swapping leaks resources.

Strategies serialized alongside the context (e.g., in a session or cache) require all concrete strategy types to be registrable or self-contained; a strategy that references an external service or library fails to deserialize on a different deployment.
An interface that grows a method per variant (one monster interface) means every concrete strategy implements operations it does not use; the contract stops describing a coherent family.
Forcing an abstract base class when a plain function or callable suffices adds unnecessary boilerplate; prefer Callable or Protocol in dynamically typed languages.

Wrong move: ship a comparator strategy that is not a total order (inconsistent tie-breaks, subtraction overflow, unhandled nulls) -> failure: Java's TimSort throws IllegalArgumentException "Comparison method violates its general contract" mid-sort, or silently misorders on inputs the unit tests never reached -> instead: implement a strict total order, delegate nulls via Comparator.nullsFirst/Last, and property-test antisymmetry and transitivity.

Wrong move: let the comparison key be mutable data the strategy reads after insertion -> failure: TreeMap/TreeSet lookups miss entries whose ordering position silently changed -> instead: compare immutable keys, or remove and re-insert when the key changes.

Wrong move: bake request- or tenant-scoped configuration into a shared long-lived strategy instance -> failure: values leak across requests or every call pays a fresh allocation and cache misses -> instead: keep the strategy a shared, immutable object and pass request-scoped data as arguments to the operation.
